content: Clobetasol propionate is a highly potent topical corticosteroid used for the treatment of corticosteroid-responsive dermatoses in patients aged 12 years and older, and for severe plaque-type psoriasis in patients aged 16 years and older. It is available as a 0.05% emollient formulation. Common adverse reactions include itching (pruritus), skin irritation, redness (erythema), inflammation of hair follicles (folliculitis), cracking and fissuring of the skin, numbness in the fingers, tenderness in the elbows, skin thinning (atrophy), and visible small blood vessels (telangiectasia). The treatment duration should not exceed two consecutive weeks, and the total dosage should not exceed 50 grams per week. For moderate to severe plaque-type psoriasis, treatment beyond four consecutive weeks is not recommended. Pediatric use under 16 years of age is not advised due to the risk of systemic absorption and potential side effects. Clobetasol propionate should be applied to the affected skin areas twice daily, with gentle and complete rubbing. Hands should be washed after each application. It should not be used with occlusive dressings unless directed by a physician. Systemic absorption of clobetasol propionate can suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, potentially leading to adrenal insufficiency. This risk is higher with prolonged use, application over large surface areas, use under occlusion, or in patients with altered skin barriers or liver failure. Pediatric patients are particularly susceptible due to their higher skin surface area-to-body mass ratio. Adverse effects from systemic absorption may include Cushing's syndrome, hyperglycemia, and unmasking of latent diabetes mellitus. Local adverse reactions, such as skin atrophy, striae, telangiectasia, burning, itching, dryness, folliculitis, acneiform eruptions, hypopigmentation, hypertrichosis, perioral dermatitis, allergic contact dermatitis, secondary infections, and miliaria, may occur, especially with prolonged or occlusive use. Clobetasol propionate is contraindicated in patients with acne vulgaris, rosacea, or perioral dermatitis. Allergic contact dermatitis should be suspected if healing does not occur, and patch testing may confirm the diagnosis. If skin infections are present, appropriate antifungal or antibacterial agents should be used, and clobetasol should be discontinued until the infection is controlled. During pregnancy, clobetasol propionate should only be used if the potential benefit justifies the potential risk to the fetus. It has been shown to be teratogenic in animal studies when administered systemically or dermally. Nursing mothers should exercise caution, as systemic corticosteroids can appear in human milk and may suppress growth or interfere with endogenous corticosteroid production in infants. Clobetasol propionate is not recommended for use in pediatric patients under 12 years of age. In elderly patients, dose selection should be cautious due to potential differences in response. There is no specific FDA guidance on its use in gender, racial populations, renal or hepatic impairment, or immunocompromised patients. The mechanism of action involves anti-inflammatory, antipruritic, and vasoconstrictive properties, likely mediated by the induction of phospholipase A2 inhibitory proteins (lipocortins), which reduce the release of arachidonic acid, a precursor of inflammatory mediators like prostaglandins and leukotrienes. Clobetasol propionate has not been evaluated for carcinogenic potential in long-term animal studies. It was non-mutagenic in several test systems. Fertility studies in rats showed no significant effects on males, but high doses in females resulted in increased resorbed embryos and fewer live fetuses. The medication should be stored between 59°F and 86°F (15°C and 30°C) and should not be refrigerated. It is for external use only and should not come into contact with the eyes. Therapy should be discontinued once control is achieved, and if no improvement is seen within two weeks, the diagnosis should be reassessed.
